messages.text: What is eye diagram, and which product-related measurement decisions depend on understanding it?

A formal general definition of “eye diagram” is not provided, but the passages operationally treat it as a signal-integrity view whose “eye opening” is judged by eye height and eye width, including post-equalization PCIe eye-height and eye-width requirements [2].  
In PCIe context, eye opening is a pass/fail-style measurement because a PCIe redriver output eye opening must be greater than or equal to the listed values for its generation [2].  
PCIe Gen3 requires extrapolated eye height after EQ of 25 mV and minimum eye width after EQ of 0.3 UI, or 37.5 ps [2].  
PCIe Gen4 requires extrapolated eye height after EQ of 15 ± 1.5 mV and minimum eye width after EQ of 0.3 UI, or 18.75 ± 0.55 ps [2].  
PCIe Gen5 requires extrapolated eye height after EQ of 15 ± 1.5 mV and minimum eye width after EQ of 0.3 UI, or 9.375 ± 0.5 ps [2].  
The PCIe eye-width and eye-height measurements are taken after post-equalization and before 3-tap DFE blocks [2].  
Understanding the eye diagram also affects PCB routing and material decisions, because different fiberglass/epoxy exposure in a differential pair can create intra-pair skew and degrade the differential eye diagram seen by the receiver [1].  
In the R&S high-speed PCB/PCBA signal-integrity flow, raw evidence lists “IL/Xtalk/Eye diagram” together with “TDR Impedance,” “Stackup Planner,” and “TL Calculator” [66].  
In R&S PCB test solutions for PCB Fabricator and System House, “Eye diagram” is explicitly part of the Material/Stackup selection stage, alongside IL, DK/DF, roughness, impedance, Xtalk, and TL modeling [15].  
Therefore, one product-related decision is whether a PCB material/stackup selection workflow must include eye-diagram evaluation in addition to IL, DK/DF, roughness, impedance, Xtalk, and TL modeling [15].  
Another product-related decision is whether the high-speed PCB/PCBA SI workflow should include eye-diagram analysis together with IL/Xtalk, TDR impedance, stackup planning, and transmission-line calculation, as shown in the raw R&S slide text [66].  
For R&S instrumentation, the R&S ZNA software option R&S®ZNA-K20 is “Extended time domain analysis including eye diagram,” and it requires R&S®ZNA-K2 Time domain analysis [34].  
Thus, an R&S ZNA configuration decision that depends on needing eye-diagram understanding is whether to include ZNA-K20, and whether the prerequisite ZNA-K2 is also present [34].

PCIe Gen5 high-speed PCB layout › Dk / Df 與 fiber weave skew
- [[snla426]]（June 2023）說 routing differential signals 時，每條 trace 會因 [[fiberglass weave]] 與 [[epoxy]] 的 static permittivity（εr）差異，而經歷不同 dielectric constants 與 signal velocities。
- [[snla426]]（June 2023）說 fiberglass weave 的 εr 約為 6，epoxy 的 εr 約為 3。
- [[snla426]]（June 2023）說 fiber glass laminate 中的 holes 或 openings 會造成 εr 與 loss tangent（Df）差異。
- [[snla426]]（June 2023）說 εr 與 Df 差異會在 signal bandwidth 的不同頻率上造成 transmission media 的 [[return loss]] 或 [[insertion loss]] resonance / anti-resonance。
- [[snla426]]（June 2023）說 differential pair 兩條 signal 若經過不同 fiberglass / epoxy 比例，會產生 [[intra-pair skew]]，並劣化 receiver 看到的 differential eye diagram。
- [[snla426]]（June 2023）說 fiber weave skew 會造成 duty cycle distortion、AC common-mode voltage noise 與 EMI issues。

A formal general definition of “eye diagram” is not provided, but the passages operationally treat it as a signal-integrity view whose “eye opening” is judged by eye height and eye width, including post-equalization PCIe eye-height and eye-width requirements [2].  
In PCIe context, eye opening is a pass/fail-style measurement because a PCIe redriver output eye opening must be greater than or equal to the listed values for its generation [2].  
PCIe Gen3 requires extrapolated eye height after EQ of 25 mV and minimum eye width after EQ of 0.3 UI, or 37.5 ps [2].  
PCIe Gen4 requires extrapolated eye height after EQ of 15 ± 1.5 mV and minimum eye width after EQ of 0.3 UI, or 18.75 ± 0.55 ps [2].  
PCIe Gen5 requires extrapolated eye height after EQ of 15 ± 1.5 mV and minimum eye width after EQ of 0.3 UI, or 9.375 ± 0.5 ps [2].  
The PCIe eye-width and eye-height measurements are taken after post-equalization and before 3-tap DFE blocks [2].  
Understanding the eye diagram also affects PCB routing and material decisions, because different fiberglass/epoxy exposure in a differential pair can create intra-pair skew and degrade the differential eye diagram seen by the receiver [1].  
In the R&S high-speed PCB/PCBA signal-integrity flow, raw evidence lists “IL/Xtalk/Eye diagram” together with “TDR Impedance,” “Stackup Planner,” and “TL Calculator” [66].  
In R&S PCB test solutions for PCB Fabricator and System House, “Eye diagram” is explicitly part of the Material/Stackup selection stage, alongside IL, DK/DF, roughness, impedance, Xtalk, and TL modeling [15].  
Therefore, one product-related decision is whether a PCB material/stackup selection workflow must include eye-diagram evaluation in addition to IL, DK/DF, roughness, impedance, Xtalk, and TL modeling [15].  
Another product-related decision is whether the high-speed PCB/PCBA SI workflow should include eye-diagram analysis together with IL/Xtalk, TDR impedance, stackup planning, and transmission-line calculation, as shown in the raw R&S slide text [66].  
For R&S instrumentation, the R&S ZNA software option R&S®ZNA-K20 is “Extended time domain analysis including eye diagram,” and it requires R&S®ZNA-K2 Time domain analysis [34].  
Thus, an R&S ZNA configuration decision that depends on needing eye-diagram understanding is whether to include ZNA-K20, and whether the prerequisite ZNA-K2 is also present [34].
